extracted.intended_audience: academics, grant applicants, program officers, and researchers studying peer review and research funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for how grant/fellowship panels select, evaluate, and deliberate on proposals, including program objectives, panel composition, roles of program officers/screeners/panelists, and evaluative criteria used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program objectives as evaluative frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding programs state objectives on their websites and these objectives influence panel deliberations; panelists may be asked how proposals measure up to such explicit goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs can set distinctive goals (e.g., IDFR’s agenda-setting aim for more theoretical, interdisciplinary, comparative area studies; WWNFF’s aim to “encourage original and significant research about women that crosses disciplinary, regional, or cultural boundaries”). Program officers may ask panelists to 'factor in' program priorities or diversity goals during evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical research quality (formal evaluative criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical criteria that address the quality of the proposed research (summarized in the book's Table 2.1 and aligned with typical agency criteria such as NSF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These publicly stated technical criteria assess the quality/technical proficiency of proposals; making them public increases accountability and makes success dependent on demonstrable technical competence. (Detailed treatment deferred to Chapter 5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies consider the interdisciplinarity of proposals as an explicit evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some programs were created specifically to promote interdisciplinary, comparative, or cross-disciplinary work (IDFR, WWNFF). Proposal reviewers may be instructed to value work that crosses disciplinary boundaries or combines disciplinary training with area/language/cultural expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding organizations consider the diversity (by institution, discipline, geographic location, race/ethnicity, and gender) of applicants when distributing awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers may encourage panelists to 'factor in' various kinds of diversity; panel composition and target populations also reflect diversity goals. Diversity can be an explicit priority alongside technical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition: balance and complementary coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should be composed to provide 'balance in perspectives' and complementary coverage of wide areas of scholarship and disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice panels should include some women, individuals teaching outside the Northeast, and people from nonelite institutions, and ideally some people of color (depending on panel size). Composition aims to ensure legitimacy through breadth and openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of evaluators (panelists and screeners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screeners and panelists are typically 'accomplished tenured faculty or independent scholars of comparable attainment' often drawn from databases and consultation with boards and learned societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many evaluators are former award recipients or field experts; boards often approve selections. Program officers consult networks and trusted insiders to identify candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities/dispositions of panelists
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists should be 'tough-minded but also broad-minded' and are expected to be 'distinguished scholars' who can learn from others and judge work rigorously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists are expected to do careful reading and participate in a full day's discussion; desirable personal qualities include openness to new work, willingness to learn, and commitment to establishing standards of quality nationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical interpersonal qualities of panelists
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers look for panelists who demonstrate 'breadth, articulatedness, confidence, and friendliness,' along with flexibility and the ability to work quickly (and, bluntly, 'not be an asshole').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good interpersonal skills are valued because panelists must negotiate face-to-face, help maintain a collegial tone, and avoid entrenched conflicts that impede deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and responsibilities of the program officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers run competitions: select screeners and panelists, communicate with and direct them, supervise organization/distribution of applications, and preside over or appoint panel chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They set the tone of panels (facilitate interactions, promote collegiality, diffuse tensions, ensure efficacy, perform 'repair work'), instruct panelists about evaluation criteria and priorities, and exercise indirect agenda-setting power (e.g., terminate panelists, promote screeners). They do not force panelists to follow guidelines but can influence outcomes via composition and agenda control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and function of screeners (prescreening/coarse sorting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screeners prescreen applications within their general field (often two screeners per applicant) and their scores/comments are used to eliminate roughly 50% of proposals overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screeners perform 'coarse sorting' rather than fine distinctions; they are given several weeks but typically little formal guidance. The amount/care of screener comments varies from brief rankings to a few lines of notes; program officers may re-invite careful screeners and panelists may optionally 'check' screener work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-deliberation rankings and scoring scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists assign pre-meeting rankings to each finalist (typically on a scale of one to five or A to E) based on reading applications and materials prior to deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rankings form the basis for panel discussion; panelists usually have about a month to read many proposals (from ~18 up to ~80) and must balance this work with other obligations. Time pressure influences depth of reading (e.g., allotting ~40 minutes per proposal in one account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panelists’ evaluative tasks during deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists build cases in favor of or against candidates, discuss evaluations with colleagues, compare and assess a wide range of materials, and make final recommendations concerning recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires familiarity with several literatures, the ability to absorb new information from others, and the capacity to offer convincing support for determinations. Consensus reached after discussion is treated as establishing standards and legitimating awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards fairness and guarding against arbitrary criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists and program officers monitor for arbitrary or idiosyncratic standards (e.g., eliminating proposals for lacking a specific time schedule) and may revisit eliminations judged excessively harsh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality control mechanisms include panel review of screener eliminations and program officer oversight of screener performance; fairness and non-arbitrariness are emphasized as part of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and procedural norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidentiality guidelines constrain what panelists can say publicly and shape the conduct of deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality supports candid discussion; procedural ceremonies and public statements about rules help legitimate the process ('myths and ceremonies'), while behind-the-scenes social dynamics also shape outcomes (addressed elsewhere in the book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy goals: rigorous, well-informed, venturesome, fair process
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding organizations aim for panels to be perceived as rigorous, well-informed, venturesome, and fair, with panel deliberations contributing to national standards of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation of panelists and of the funding organization, plus traditions of funding significant work, are leveraged to sustain legitimacy; program officers cultivate evaluators who identify with this culture of excellence.
